conservative: This conservative variant anchors most heavily on classic downside credit signals: debt-to-income, revolving utilization, interest rate/LC grade, FICO band, prior delinquencies, and stability markers like income, employment length, and credit history. Its posture is clearly caution-first and asymmetrically sensitive to negative indicators, often treating subprime-leaning pricing, high utilization, or mixed profiles as sufficient reason to lean toward charge-off even when there are meaningful compensating strengths. A recurring pattern is that it explicitly frames decisions around “mixed signals” and then resolves ambiguity by defaulting to the riskier outcome, especially when leverage or pricing looks stretched. Its main blind spot is a tendency to overweight broad risk labels such as grade, interest rate, and utilization relative to stronger repayment-capacity evidence, though in a few cases it swings the other way when the file looks generally clean on surface credit metrics. The reasoning feels fairly structured and somewhat templated, but still grounded in the specific loan’s feature mix rather than being purely generic.
chain_of_thought: This chain-of-thought variant consistently anchors on a familiar credit stack: grade/interest rate, FICO, recent delinquency indicators, revolving utilization, DTI, income versus payment, and then secondary stability cues like homeownership, employment length, verification, and credit history length. Its posture is broadly balanced but slightly credit-bureau-trusting, often letting clean historical file signals and capacity markers outweigh softer warning signs, while becoming notably stricter when delinquencies are recent and explicitly repeated. Across samples, it uses an additive “risk signals vs protective factors” ledger, with strong weight on absence of bankruptcies/public records and long credit history, and it tends to interpret debt consolidation or manageable payment size as reassuring. A recurring tendency is to underreact to layered medium-risk combinations—especially long terms, weaker grades, elevated rates, and moderate delinquency/utilization—if income, FICO, and file cleanliness look respectable. The reasoning feels fairly specific to each loan because it cites concrete values and case details, but the structure is highly templated and formulaic, following the same compare-and-offset pattern almost every time.
few_shot: This few-shot variant reasons in a fairly checklist-driven way, anchoring most heavily on FICO band, LendingClub grade/interest rate, recent delinquencies, revolving utilization, income verification/strength, and the length of employment and credit history. Its posture is broadly balanced but slightly conservative when multiple risk flags stack up, especially high utilization plus weaker grade/rate plus delinquency history; at the same time, it will readily offset those negatives with “compensating factors” like solid income, clean bankruptcy/public-record history, and long tenure. A distinctive pattern is that it treats clean traditional credit signals as highly reassuring and often frames decisions as a tradeoff between a few negatives and an otherwise stable profile. It seems somewhat less sensitive to interactions among risk factors at the tails, sometimes overtrusting decent FICO/income when a loan later charges off, or overpenalizing very high rate/grade/utilization even when the loan is ultimately repaid. The language feels fairly specific to each loan’s feature mix, but the argumentative structure is templated: cite key positives, acknowledge a couple negatives, then conclude with an “overall profile” judgment.
top_features_only: This variant reasons in a stripped-down, feature-priority way, repeatedly anchoring on a small set of classic credit signals: grade/interest rate, FICO band, debt-to-income, revolving utilization, delinquencies/public records, income relative to loan size, and credit-history length. Its posture is fairly balanced but somewhat scorecard-like, often weighing a few strong positives against a few obvious negatives and then choosing the side that feels more dominant. A clear pattern is that it treats loan grade, term length, recent delinquency, and utilization as especially decisive on riskier files, while on safer-looking files it leans heavily on clean recent credit behavior and affordability cues. It tends to underuse richer contextual nuance beyond those top factors, so its mistakes often look like cases where a superficially clean profile overrides latent risk, or where a cluster of headline risk flags overwhelms otherwise stable repayment capacity. Overall, the reasoning feels somewhat templated and formulaic, with specific feature references for each loan but a very consistent “list positives, list negatives, then net them out” structure across samples.
structured_4factor: This variant has a distinctly four-bucket style: it repeatedly anchors on repayment capacity, credit quality/history, current debt stress, and loan structure, often explicitly balancing income vs. monthly payment, DTI, revolving utilization, FICO, delinquencies/public records, and grade/term. Its risk posture is fairly conservative and additive—negative signals like high utilization, recent delinquencies, bankruptcies, long 60-month terms, and weaker grades are treated as compounding risks that can outweigh otherwise solid income or long credit history. Across samples, it shows a systematic tendency to trust clean derogatory history and low DTI as strong positives, while heavily penalizing visible stress markers and structural loan risk, especially when multiple red flags appear together. A mild blind spot is that it can overreact to surface credit-risk flags even when broader repayment performance is stable, and it sometimes seems to underappreciate cases where good credit profile masks eventual default. The reasoning feels semi-templated rather than deeply bespoke: each case is framed as a structured tradeoff among the same recurring factors, with only modest tailoring to the specific loan.
risk_signal_guide: This variant reasons in a checklist-like way, anchoring most heavily on loan grade and interest rate, then on a recurring cluster of credit cleanliness signals: revolving utilization, DTI, delinquencies, bankruptcies/public records, income verification, and sometimes FICO, employment length, and credit history length. Its posture is fairly conservative and adverse-signal-driven, especially when it sees very high utilization or any derogatory records, which it often treats as decisive even when other parts of the file look stable. It also appears to carry some priors about loan purpose, tending to frame debt_consolidation and credit_card as relatively safer and medical as riskier. Across samples, it systematically balances positives and negatives in a formulaic “offset” structure, but it may overweight conspicuous red flags and underreact to more subtle combinations that still imply trouble. Overall, the reasoning feels somewhat templated rather than deeply case-specific: the same feature hierarchy and contrastive phrasing recur, with only modest tailoring to the individual loan.
